subject: predict() using stPGOcc model in spOccupancy

messages.author: 1614faf2ff7c8fc4
messages.subject: predict() using stPGOcc model in spOccupancy
parts:
Hello,

I'm trying to use the model results from an stPGOcc analysis (through the spOccupancy package in R) to predict responses for detection and occurrence in a broader landscape.

I had a few questions regarding the build of the X.0 object directly from the data object used in the original model.

The data object of the original model contains the data matrix 'y', 'occ.covs', 'det.covs', and the coords. In the case of missing data, the data object can be used in the stPGOcc model after removing NA rows in the 'y' data matrix. This is the model procedure I've followed - by subsetting the 'data' object to generate a 'data_NAremoved' object (or list of lists) to run the analysis. I would now like to predict occurrence and detection from the model on all sites contained in the original 'data' object. 

I wanted to know if it would be possible to subset the 'data' object in a manner that allows for the generation of the X.0 design matrix directly, rather than building the X.0 matrix from scratch. The considerations would be to scale the covariates properly, based on the mean and sd values of the scaled covariates used in the original model, and only 'predict' on the new sites, or to 'predict' using the full dataset (effectively a double prediction for the sites used in the creation of the model).

I'm having trouble with the creation of X.0 from scratch, and was not able to properly follow using the example code found in https://rdrr.io/github/doserjef/spOccupancy/man/predict.stPGOcc.html

messages.subject: Re: predict() using stPGOcc model in spOccupancy
parts:
A few more details with code.

#Read/Import model
 modelout.sp_1 <- readRDS("TopModel_600x25_27022024.rds")

#data structure base
num_sites <- nrow(data_msom$y)
num_months_per_season <- 4
num_seasons <- 24
num_covariates<- 4 #inc intercept

# Determine dimensions for X0
X.0_dims <- c(num_sites, num_seasons, num_covariates)

#covars - scaled using model scale values
predScaled_ntl_s <- as.data.frame((lapply(1:ncol(data_msom$occ.covs$ntl_s), function(i) {
  (data_msom$occ.covs$ntl_s[, i] - mean(data_msom_NARemoved$occ.covs$ntl_s[, i])) / sd(data_msom_NARemoved$occ.covs$ntl_s[, i])})))
    colnames(predScaled_ntl_s) <- colnames(data_msom_NARemoved$occ.covs$ntl_s)

predScaled_lstd_s <- as.data.frame((lapply(1:ncol(data_msom$occ.covs$lstd_s), function(i) {
  (data_msom$occ.covs$lstd_s[, i] - mean(data_msom_NARemoved$occ.covs$lstd_s[, i])) / sd(data_msom_NARemoved$occ.covs$lstd_s[, i])})))
    colnames(predScaled_lstd_s) <- colnames(data_msom_NARemoved$occ.covs$lstd_s)

predScaled_evi_s <- as.data.frame((lapply(1:ncol(data_msom$occ.covs$evi_s), function(i) {
  (data_msom$occ.covs$evi_s[, i] - mean(data_msom_NARemoved$occ.covs$evi_s[, i])) / sd(data_msom_NARemoved$occ.covs$evi_s[, i])})))
    colnames(predScaled_evi_s) <- colnames(data_msom_NARemoved$occ.covs$evi_s)

#conversion to matrices # Reshape the monthly/obs level matrix into a three-dimensional array
predScaled_ntl_s_0 <- predScaled_ntl_s %>% as.matrix(rownames = T)
  predScaled_ntl_s_0 <- array(predScaled_ntl_s_0, dim = (c(num_sites, num_months_per_season, num_seasons)))

predScaled_lstd_s_0 <- predScaled_lstd_s %>% as.matrix(rownames = T)
  predScaled_lstd_s_0 <- array(predScaled_lstd_s_0, dim = (c(num_sites, num_months_per_season, num_seasons)))

predScaled_evi_s_0 <- predScaled_evi_s %>% as.matrix(rownames = T)
  predScaled_evi_s_0 <- array(predScaled_evi_s_0, dim = (c(num_sites, num_months_per_season, num_seasons))) 

# Coordinates for prediction - all coords of all sites
  predict_coords <- data_msom$coords

#creating prediction design matrix for Occurance
  #order: "scale(ntl_s) + scale(lstd_s) + scale(evi_s)"(from the original occ.formula)
X.0_occ_a <- cbind(1, predScaled_ntl_s_0, predScaled_lstd_s_0, predScaled_evi_s_0)
colnames(X.0_occ_a) <- c("","ntl_s","lstd_s","evi_s")
X.0_occ_b <- array(X.0_occ_a, dim = X.0_dims)
X.0_occ <- aperm(X.0_occ_b, c(1, 2, 3))


#prediction for occurance
out.pred_occ <- predict(modelout.sp_1, X.0_occ, predict_coords,
                        t.cols = c(1, 4,7), #set 1 - monsoon
                        n.omp.threads = 8, type = 'occupancy')
summary(out.pred_occ)

mean.psi <- apply(out.pred_occ$psi.0.samples, 2, mean)
sd.psi <- apply(out.pred_occ$psi.0.samples, 2, sd)


I'm unsure if the creation of X.0 is correct, as the output results do not seem to contain any predicted values. I also frequently run in fatal errors, where the R Session ttterminates when the prediction is run.

Any guidance would be really helpful!

messages.author: 9723aac8fc0c9507
messages.subject: Re: predict() using stPGOcc model in spOccupancy
parts:
Hi Anubhav,

Yes, it is possible to take the object formatted in the format for the "data" argument of stPGOcc() and manipulate it into the X.0 design matrix for prediction. You can predict either at just the new sites, or at all sites together. I've attached a script that shows how to do that using the "hbefTrends" data set included in the package. In the script, I first load the full data set, remove 100 sites from the data set to generate a new data set, fit the model with the new data set, and then predict occupancy probability across all sites in the original data set after manipulating the object into the required format for the X.0 design matrix. You should be able to take pretty much the same approach for predicting detection probability.

After a quick glance, I don't see anything immediately wrong with the code you attached, but there could be something I'm missing without being able to run it with the data myself. As far as R terminating when the prediction is running, that could be due to your computer running out of memory. If you're predicting across a large number of sites, then the resulting object from predict() will be very large. The size of the prediction object also depends on how many MCMC samples you save from the model run. The larger the number of samples you are saving the bigger the object will be from predict(), and the more memory you will need to do the prediction. If this is the problem, one way to get around this is to break up the prediction into small chunks, where you only predict at a subset of the locations at a time.

Hope that helps! If you can't get things to work after looking through the script, then feel free to send me (off-list) your code and data needed to reproduce the problems.

Jeff
